nodes.summary: Every congestion game with finitely many players, resources and strategies, and at least one strategy for every player, has a pure Nash equilibrium.
nodes.title: Congestion games have pure Nash equilibria

nodes.summary: A congestion game has players $i \in I$, a finite set $R$ of resources, for every player a set $S_i$ of strategies, each strategy $a$ using a set $R_i(a) \subseteq R$ of resources, and for every resource $e$ a delay function $d_e : \mathbb N \to \mathbb R$: when $n$ players use $e$, each of them pays $d_e(n)$ for it.
nodes.title: Congestion game

nodes.summary: In a congestion game, the cost of player $i$ at the profile $s$ is $c_i(s) = \sum_{e \in R_i(s_i)} d_e(n_e(s))$, the sum of the delays of the resources it uses.
nodes.title: Cost of a player in a congestion game

nodes.summary: In the fair cost-sharing game with $k$ players and finitely many strategies, nonempty for every player, there is a pure Nash equilibrium $s$ whose network costs at most $H(k)$ times the network of every profile $t$: Taking $t$ optimal, the price of stability is at most $H(k) = O(\log k)$; the bound is tight.
nodes.title: Price of stability of fair cost sharing is at most H(k)

nodes.summary: Every game with finitely many (and at least one) strategy profiles that has an exact potential has a pure Nash equilibrium.
nodes.title: Finite potential games have pure Nash equilibria

nodes.summary: For the fair cost-sharing game, Rosenthal's potential is $\Phi(s) = \sum_e c_e\, H(n_e(s))$, where $H(n) = 1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac1n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number.
nodes.title: Rosenthal's potential for fair cost sharing

nodes.summary: In the fair cost-sharing network design game, player $i$ chooses a strategy $a \in S_i$ that uses a set $R_i(a)$ of edges, every edge $e$ has a cost $c_e \ge 0$, and the cost of each edge is split equally among the players using it: player $i$ pays $\sum_{e \in R_i(s_i)} c_e / n_e(s)$. In the network design setting $S_i$ is the set of $s_i$–$t_i$ paths of a graph.
nodes.title: Fair cost-sharing game

nodes.summary: A profile $t$ is reached from $s$ by an improving move if some player $i$ changes only its own strategy, $t = (a, s_{-i})$, and strictly lowers its cost, $c_i(t) < c_i(s)$. Sequences of improving moves are improvement paths; best-response dynamics is a special case.
nodes.title: Improving move

nodes.summary: Every congestion game is an exact potential game, with Rosenthal's potential $\Phi(s) = \sum_e \sum_{k=1}^{n_e(s)} d_e(k)$ as potential. No assumption on the delays is needed.
nodes.title: Rosenthal's theorem

nodes.summary: A function $\Phi$ on strategy profiles is an exact potential for the costs $c_i$ if every unilateral deviation changes the deviating player's cost by exactly the change in $\Phi$: for every profile $s$, player $i$ and strategy $a \in S_i$. A game with an exact potential is an (exact) potential game.
nodes.title: Exact potential

nodes.summary: If $\Phi$ is an exact potential and the profile $s$ minimises $\Phi$ over all profiles, then $s$ is a pure Nash equilibrium.
nodes.title: Potential minimisers are Nash equilibria

nodes.summary: Consider a strategic game with players $i \in I$, strategy sets $S_i$ and costs $c_i : \prod_j S_j \to \mathbb R$, which each player wants to minimise. A strategy profile $s$ is a pure Nash equilibrium if no player can lower its cost by changing only its own strategy: $c_i(s) \le c_i(a, s_{-i})$ for every player $i$ and every $a \in S_i$, where $(a, s_{-i})$ is $s$ with the $i$-th coordinate replaced by $a$.
nodes.title: Pure Nash equilibrium

nodes.summary: The load of resource $e$ at $s$ equals the number of players other than $i$ using $e$, plus $1$ if player $i$'s strategy uses $e$ and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Load splits over one player

nodes.summary: The number of players other than $i$ using resource $e$ does not change when player $i$ changes its strategy.
nodes.title: Load from the others ignores the deviator

nodes.summary: In a congestion game, the number of players other than $i$ whose strategy at the profile $s$ uses resource $e$.
nodes.title: Load from the other players

nodes.summary: In a congestion game, the load $n_e(s)$ of resource $e$ at the profile $s$ is the number of players whose strategy uses $e$.
nodes.title: Load of a resource

nodes.summary: If $\Phi$ is an exact potential and $t$ is reached from $s$ by an improving move, then $\Phi(t) < \Phi(s)$.
nodes.title: Improving moves decrease the potential

nodes.summary: In the fair cost-sharing game, the cost of the network built at $s$ is at most Rosenthal's potential $\Phi(s)$, because $H(n) \ge 1$ for $n \ge 1$ and $c_e \ge 0$.
nodes.title: Network cost is at most the potential

nodes.summary: The cost of the network built at the profile $s$ of a fair cost-sharing game is the total cost $\sum_{e : n_e(s) > 0} c_e$ of the edges used by at least one player. It is the sum of the players' payments.
nodes.title: Cost of the built network

nodes.summary: For every player $i$ and profile $s$, Rosenthal's potential is where $m_e$ is the number of players other than $i$ using $e$. The first term does not depend on $s_i$.
nodes.title: Rosenthal's potential splits over one player

nodes.summary: In the fair cost-sharing game with $k$ players, Rosenthal's potential satisfies $\Phi(s) \le H(k) \cdot \sum_{e : n_e(s) > 0} c_e$, because every load is at most $k$.
nodes.title: Potential is at most H(k) times the network cost

nodes.summary: The fair cost-sharing game is the congestion game with delays $d_e(n) = c_e / n$.
nodes.title: Fair cost sharing as a congestion game

nodes.summary: In a game with finitely many strategy profiles and an exact potential, the improving-move relation is well founded: there is no infinite sequence of profiles each reached from the previous one by an improving move. In particular best-response dynamics, from any starting profile, reaches a pure Nash equilibrium after finitely many steps.
nodes.title: Finite improvement property

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
